integrityMatters.title: High Court ruling that Senator Gallagher was ineligible to be elected at the 2016 election under section 44(i) of the Constitution (Re Gallagher)
integrityMatters.organisation: High Court of Australia sitting as the Court of Disputed Returns, on a reference from the Senate
integrityMatters.description: Senator Gallagher was a British citizen by descent. She signed a declaration of renunciation on 20 April 2016, lodged with the United Kingdom Home Office on 26 April 2016, but the Home Office did not register the renunciation until 16 August 2016, after nominations for the 2 July 2016 election had closed. On 6 December 2017, at her request, the Senate referred questions about her eligibility to the Court of Disputed Returns. On 9 May 2018 the High Court unanimously held that she was a citizen of a foreign power when nominated and was therefore incapable of being chosen as a senator under section 44(i), and that the exception for cases where foreign law irremediably prevents renunciation did not apply. The vacancy was filled by a special count and she returned to the Senate at the 2019 election. A section 44 ineligibility finding concerns constitutional eligibility; the court made no finding about her honesty or conduct.

statusHistory.note: At her own request, the Senate resolved to refer questions concerning her eligibility at the 2016 election to the Court of Disputed Returns.

The Full Court (Kiefel CJ, Bell, Gageler, Keane, Nettle, Gordon and Edelman JJ) unanimously answered that there was a vacancy in her seat by reason of section 44(i), to be filled by a special count of the ballot papers.

Following the special count, David Smith was declared elected to the ACT Senate vacancy. The Parliament of Australia's record states 'Election ruled void 9.5.2018 under section 44 (i) of the Constitution'.

integrityMatters.outcome: Court's answers: whether section 44(i) created a vacancy, 'Yes'; how it should be filled, 'by a special count of the ballot papers'. The Parliament of Australia records her 2016 election as 'ruled void 9.5.2018 under section 44 (i) of the Constitution'. She was elected again at the 2019 election.

integrityMatters.title: Federal Court adverse-action claim by Mr Marles's former chief of staff against the Commonwealth, Mr Marles and the Prime Minister's chief of staff, settled without findings
integrityMatters.organisation: Federal Court of Australia (proceeding under the Fair Work Act 2009)
integrityMatters.description: Jo Tarnawsky, chief of staff to the Deputy Prime Minister, said in October 2024 that she had raised a complaint of bullying and harassment by a senior colleague in Mr Marles's office and had subsequently been kept out of her role and left on leave. She did not allege that Mr Marles personally bullied her. In November 2024 she filed a Federal Court claim under the Fair Work Act alleging adverse action in response to her complaint, naming the Commonwealth, Mr Marles and the Prime Minister's chief of staff as respondents. In March 2025 the parties settled on confidential terms and the proceeding was discontinued; a government spokesperson said no adverse findings had been made against any person. There is no judgment.

statusHistory.note: Statement of claim filed in the Federal Court alleging adverse action under the Fair Work Act. Ms Tarnawsky had said publicly in October 2024 that she was sidelined after making a bullying complaint about a colleague.
Dispute settled on confidential terms before any hearing; the proceeding was discontinued. A government spokesperson said no adverse findings had been made against any person.

integrityMatters.outcome: Settled confidentially before any hearing; no judgment and no findings. Government spokesperson, 21 March 2025: 'The welfare of all staff has been front of mind and remains so. The proceeding will be discontinued.' The spokesperson noted that no adverse findings had been made against any person.
